The remaining phrases are to be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, is there [any such thing]? No.
"Because it has no substance.
And yet, does it not exist? "No."
Because it can obscure the truth;
the remaining phrases are to be understood by analogy with this.
Second, the demonstration of the fault of clinging.
If one reckons that True Suchness (tathatā) is exclusively existent,
there are two faults:
first, the fault of permanence.
This means: because it does not follow conditions;
because it is not concealed while in a state of defilement;
and because it does not depend on a revealing cause.
This would immediately entail the fallacy of eternalism.
Question: In all the holy teachings, it is stated that True Suchness (tathatā) is an immutably constant reality.
If it does not follow conditions, how can it be a fault?
Answer: When the Sages describe True Suchness as "immutable," this refers to the time when it follows conditions to become defiled or pure.
It constantly manifests as both defiled and pure without losing its own essence;
this is precisely the permanence that is not different from impermanence,
and is termed "inconceivable permanence."
This does not mean that all phenomena are inactive and utterly static as they are conceived by the mundane mind.
If one were to claim that all phenomena are inactive and static,
this would be a conceptual construction of the mundane mind and would thus deviate from true permanence.
Because that true permanence is a permanence not different from impermanence—
this permanence not different from impermanence transcends the realm of ordinary emotion and is therefore called "true permanence. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"That which is unstained yet stained" clarifies that the permanent is treated as impermanent.
"That which is stained yet unstained" [clarifies that the impermanent is treated as permanent].
This clarifies that when one acts with impermanence, one does not lose that constancy.
Question: Since the teaching speaks of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as an immutably constant reality because it is the constancy that is non-different from impermanence, [how is this so?]
Why is it that True Suchness (tathatā) is not described as impermanent on the basis of an impermanence that is not distinct from [the conventional]?
Answer: This meaning is also taught in the scriptures.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure;
it arises and ceases together with its causes."
The treatise states:
"The intrinsically pure mind,
stirred by the wind of ignorance, becomes the defiled mind and so forth."
Based on this teaching and reasoning,
it is known that because True Suchness is not different from impermanence itself,
its essence remains concealed in accordance with conditions.
This is not existence.
Question: True Suchness is a dharma that is neither arising nor ceasing.
Since it is not different from the permanence of impermanence, it is therefore described as permanent.
Because it is impermanent in a manner that is not distinct from the ordinary,
it can be said to be impermanent; furthermore,
it may also be understood as a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing in dependence upon others.
"Should it not also be possible to have the meaning of 'impermanence that is not different from permanence' and 'permanence that is not different from impermanence'?
Answer: It is indeed possible. Why is this?"
Because the phenomena of dependent origination are impermanent, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
and it is precisely through this absence of intrinsic nature that they constitute dependent origination.
Therefore, impermanence is not something distinct from the nature of things.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Neither arising nor ceasing is the meaning of impermanence.
This means that what is not different from permanence constitutes impermanence.
Furthermore, since all dependent origination is itself devoid of intrinsic nature,
it is not the case that one must first extinguish dependent origination before its lack of nature can be spoken of;
this is precisely the permanence that is not different from impermanence.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Form is itself emptiness;
it is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness."
It is further said:
"Sentient beings are themselves nirvāṇa;
they do not undergo further extinction," and so forth.
Within this, the two meanings [of the conventional] correspond to the two meanings [of the ultimate],
as can be understood by comparison.
This is precisely the dual integration of the ultimate and the conventional, wherein the two are non-dual.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The extreme blindness and darkness of the cognitive obstacles refers to the separate apprehension of the ultimate and the conventional."
This is what is meant by that.
Therefore, if one were to hold that the true thusness is as it is described— remaining eternally quiescent—
it would not conceal its own essence in accordance with conditions, nor would it require a "revealing cause" (jñāna-hetu).
One would then fall into the error of eternalism.
Furthermore, if defilement and purity were not established in accordance with conditions,
then dharmas such as defilement and purity would have no basis.
Furthermore, if there were dharmas that existed without a basis, they would fall into the error of eternalism.
This is because both defiled and pure dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are established in dependence upon the Truth (*tattva*).
Second, the fault of [the two types of] cessation:
That which exists as a mere mental construct is not true existence;
because it is not true existence, it is the severance of existence.
Furthermore, if there were existence...
Thus, it does not follow after defilement or purity.
Since all phenomena of defilement and purity lack intrinsic nature,
the Truth likewise does not follow them, as it cannot obtain any such phenomena.
This, too, is a form of nihilism. Furthermore,
the second position— that which clings to non-existence—
likewise entails two faults.
Regarding the fault of permanence:
it means that if true suchness did not exist, birth and death would have no basis;
and for an existing phenomenon to lack a basis is precisely what constitutes permanence.
Furthermore, True Suchness and noble wisdom have no cause,
and they are likewise eternal.
Moreover, without a basis, no phenomenon can exist.
This is precisely annihilationism.
Furthermore, to cling to suchness as being non-existent is also annihilationism.
Third, those who maintain that it both exists and does not exist possess all the aforementioned faults;
namely, that true suchness is non-dual.
Yet they dualistically calculate both existence and non-existence;
that which the mind calculates as existence or non-existence does not accord with reality.
Because it loses sight of that true principle, it is nihilism.
If one were to claim that what they have conceptualized is true,
then because there is truth where there is no principle,
it would follow that it is eternal.
Regarding the fourth [position], which is neither existent nor non-existent:
when conceptual proliferation is directed toward the ultimate truth,
it is a product of deluded sentiment and thus loses sight of the true principle.
This is precisely what is meant by "severance.
Regarding conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there is no such thing as "reality" that could be called real;
because in principle there is no reality, it is "permanence."
Regarding the second [point], within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
if one clings to it as existing, there are likewise two faults.
The first is the error of permanence (*nitya-doṣa*).
This means that because an entity already exists, it does not depend on conditions;
thus, a phenomenon that exists without depending on conditions is eternal.
Furthermore, by clinging to existence, one maintains that it does not depend on conditions.
Because there can be no phenomena without depending on conditions, this is precisely cessation.
Question: If it is said that the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) has the meaning of existence, [how is this so?]
If this were the case, there would be a contradiction. Why, then,
do the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises state that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists?
Answer: When the Sage speaks of existence based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), this is precisely an existence that is not different from emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Why is this so?
Because they lack intrinsic nature due to being dependent on various conditions,
and because there is no agent within each individual condition,
it is precisely through the non-activity of conditions that dependent origination is established.
Therefore, that which exists as "not being" is called "existence through dependence on others.
This is how the Noble Ones, without moving from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), establish all phenomena.
If it is claimed that the dependent nature exists as it is expressed by words,
then it would be an existent nature through dependent origination;
yet if it were an existent nature through dependence, it could not be mutually reliant.
Because they do not rely upon one another, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is immediately destroyed.
That the dependent nature is destroyed is precisely due to the grasping at existence. Therefore:
Your mind, fearing a fall into emptiness or nihilism,
strives to establish existence;
yet you do not realize that it is because phenomena arising from conditions lack intrinsic nature.
This is because destroying dependent origination would lead to falling into nihilism and severing the basis for the dependent nature.
Second, if one clings to the view that it does not exist, there are likewise two faults.
If one were to claim that the dependent nature is a non-existent thing, [the following consequences would follow].
That which conditions does not arise.
Because it does not arise, no dharma can be obtained;
this is cessation.
Question: If it is argued that by asserting dependent origination to be empty and non-existent,
one falls into the extreme of nihilism,
why then [is this not so] within the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and other such texts?
Is it being taught that dependent origination is ultimately emptiness?
The answer is: when the Noble One speaks of dependent origination as emptiness, this is precisely an emptiness that is not different from existence.
Why is this? Because it is precisely because phenomena arise from conditions that they are said to lack intrinsic nature;
therefore, it is only that which arises from conditions which can be considered empty.
If it were not so, there would be no cause for dependent origination;
by what reason, then, could one speak of emptiness?
Therefore, the emptiness that is not different from existence is called "emptiness of dependent origination."
This is precisely the teaching on the true nature of phenomena by the Noble One Acala regarding dependent origination.
If one were to claim that dependent origination is empty merely according to its verbal expression,
then there would be no dependent origination at all.
Because there is no arising without conditions, there is no principle of emptiness.
That there is no principle of emptiness is precisely due to the attachment to emptiness.
Therefore, your intention fears falling into the view of existence.
One should resolutely establish emptiness;
it is not that one fails to realize that what lacks intrinsic nature arises dependently, for by such a view,
one would lose the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Because one loses the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one falls back into the empty states of the evil destinies within the realm of emotional clinging.
Question: If it is because the dependent nature possesses these two meanings, then what of the various masters of the preceding generations?
Regarding how each articulates a single meaning such that it harmoniously subsumes the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) without contradiction:
for what reason did later masters, such as Bhāviveka and others,
[propound their respective views]?
Do they each uphold a single meaning and refute one another?
Answer: This is a case of mutual completion, not mutual refutation. Why is this so?
For sentient beings of the final age, whose faculties gradually become dull, when they hear it said that "other-dependent" is its mode of existence,
they fail to realize that such existence is not different from emptiness;
they immediately grasp at it as being an existence in the sense of a substantial entity.
Therefore, Bhāviveka and others refute the existence of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) so as to bring it to non-existence;
only upon reaching ultimate non-existence does one truly attain that existence of the dependent nature.
If one does not reach this state of ultimate emptiness,
then the existence of the dependent nature cannot be established.
Therefore, in order to establish existence, existence itself is negated.
Furthermore, when those sentient beings hear it said that the dependent nature is ultimately empty,
because they do not realize that this is an emptiness that is not distinct from existence,
they immediately grasp it as being like what is called "emptiness" [in the sense of mere non-existence].
Therefore, Dharmapāla and others refute that [view],
asserting that emptiness exists in order to preserve illusory existence.
Only because illusory existence is established can one attain that emptiness which is not different from existence.
Because if there were cessation, it would not be true emptiness;
therefore, in order to establish emptiness, one refutes [the notion of] emptiness itself.
This is because the meaning established by Candrakīrti is that form is itself emptiness.
"Emptiness is form"—the meaning of protecting the Dharma is preserved herein.
These two meanings are fused and integrated so that the entire substance is fully encompassed.
If it were not for later masters who, through the mutual penetration of these two principles, allow the entire substance to mutually subsume one another, [this would not be possible].
There would be no way to manifest the profound dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of dependent origination;
therefore, their mutual negation results in their mutual establishment.
Consequently, to cling to the notion that [the dependent nature] is non-existent is the fault of nihilism.
Furthermore, if it is said that non-existence is the dependent nature,
then non-existence would not be a condition;
and a phenomenon that is not a condition would fall into the error of eternalism.
Regarding the third position— that it both exists and does not exist—
it possesses all the aforementioned faults;
one may infer this accordingly.
Question: According to what has been explained above,
it would be untenable to take either the existence or non-existence of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as one-sided.
If both existence and non-existence are apprehended together, it should accord with reason;
how then could there also be the aforementioned faults?
Answer: Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Although it possesses the principle of both existence and non-existence,
its entire substance is mutually pervasive such that emptiness and existence are completely integrated;
thus, it is not as one might calculate it to be "both existent and nonexistent."
This would immediately result in contradiction, possessing all the aforementioned faults.
As for the fourth [position], that which is neither existent nor non-existent,
it is likewise irrational for this to be the conditionality (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Why is this? Because the conceptual constructs of those who cling to existence and non-existence are not established;
thus, they merely assert through their own sentiments that things are neither existent nor non-existent.
This is the logical principle.
Since this is not reasonable,
it likewise possesses the aforementioned faults.
One should reflect upon this accordingly.
Thirdly, within the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva),
if one imagines that which is thoroughly imagined to be existent, there are two faults.
That is to say, if that which is grasped were truly existent,
then the principle illuminated by noble wisdom would necessarily not be empty;
it would, in other words, be permanent.
If one falsely insists that the imagined nature exists in reality,
one loses the conventional existence;
therefore, this is the fault of nihilism.
Second, if one holds that the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is non-existent for sentient beings,
then ordinary people would not differ from the noble ones in their delusion;
this would imply permanence.
Furthermore, because there are no ordinary beings, this is cessation.
Moreover, since there is neither delusion, there is also no awakening.
And because there is no awakening, there are likewise no sages.
This is also cessation.
Regarding the third point, "both existent and non-existent": since the nature is neither dualistic nor two-fold, it is both existent and non-existent.
Furthermore, to claim that existence and non-existence are identical would involve contradiction;
thus, it incurs all the aforementioned faults.
Fourth, as for that which is neither existent nor non-existent:
The conceptual proliferation of pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*) likewise possesses the aforementioned faults;
this should be understood by analogy.
This concludes the second section on the fault of clinging to establishment.
Third, to demonstrate its meaning:
True Suchness (tathatā) has the sense of "existence," because it is the basis for both delusion and awakening.
Furthermore, because it is not in vain and because it is indestructible,
the rest is as explained above.
Furthermore, suchness is the meaning of emptiness,
because it is free from characteristics and because it accords with conditions.
Because it is defiled;
the rest is as above.
Furthermore, suchness has the meaning of both existence and non-existence.
Because it is endowed with virtue;
because it possesses mastery over both the adverse and the favorable;
and because it is fused and integrated.
Furthermore, it is the meaning of being neither existent nor non-existent,
because of the non-duality of duality,
and because it cannot be definitively grasped.
The remaining [terms] should be understood by reversing the explanations above.
Second, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) has the sense of "existence," because it is established through conditions and because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The remainder is to be understood according to what precedes.
Dependence upon another is devoid of intrinsic nature,
because it is established through conditions and lacks inherent existence.
This should also be understood according to what preceded.
The meaning of "neither existent nor non-existent" based on others is that they lack intrinsic nature because they are established through conditions; this is to be understood as before.
The dependent nature has the meaning of being neither existent nor non-existent, because it is both dual and non-dual;
as with the previous case, one cannot apprehend either [extreme] alone.
Third, the imagined nature is existent.
From the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*),
the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent; from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), [it is likewise non-existent].
The parikalpita (the imagined) is both existent and non-existent,
because it is that which is grasped.
The parikalpita is neither existent nor non-existent.
Because it is that which is grasped [as the object],
the other two natures should be understood accordingly as explained above. This concludes the detailed explanation of the three natures.
Regarding the second, the general exposition:
the three natures are of one single limit; by mentioning one, all are fully encompassed.
Thus, the true and the deluded are mutually interfused.
Its nature is unobstructed.
As it is said in the *Brahmaṇaparipṛcchā-sūtra* cited in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
"World-Honored One..."
In what sense is it said that the Tathāgata perceives neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa? It is because within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva),
he does not perceive the imputed nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) or the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) as being either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Based on the meaning of non-differentiation. Why is this?
Because this dependent nature—
Through one aspect of conceptual construction, saṃsāra is established;
through one aspect of reality, nirvāṇa is established.
The commentary states:
The dependent nature is not saṃsāra,
because this nature becomes nirvāṇa through the realization of reality;
yet this nature is not nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because one portion of this nature, through conceptual differentiation, is itself saṃsāra;
therefore, it cannot be definitively stated that it is a single portion.
If one perceives that the nature of one part is not different from the other parts,
for this reason one does not perceive birth-and-death,
nor does one perceive nirvāṇa.
With this intention,
the Tathāgata answered the brāhmaṇa in this manner.
Furthermore, he said:
In the Abhidharma Sūtra, the Blessed One taught that there are three categories of phenomena: first, the defiled category; [second, the pure category;
and third, the indeterminate category].
Second, the portion of purification;
third, the portion of defilement and purification.
Based on what meaning are these three portions taught?
Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) constitutes the defiled portion,
while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) constitutes the pure portion.
The dependent nature constitutes the defiled and purified portions;
based on this meaning, the three natures are taught.
The commentary states:
In the Abhidharma-sūtra it is said:
"The nature of the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature) consists of afflictions;
the nature of the pariniṣpanna-svabhāva (the perfected nature) consists of the purified portion."
Because the dependent nature possesses two aspects and has two natures as its essence,
it is said that there are three kinds of dharmas.
First, the category of affliction;
second, the category of purification;
third, the category of both dharmas.
It is based on this meaning that this statement is made.
Furthermore, the above treatise clarifies that the True encompasses the deluded and the derivative, such that there is nothing that does not correspond [to it].
When truth and falsehood thoroughly penetrate the source of truth, the essence is entirely quiescent.
When truth and falsehood mutually penetrate, the two divisions are doubly fused in unimpeded, total inclusion.
This can be seen through reflection.
Regarding the second [section], the Dharma of the six meanings of the causal gate of conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*),
this meaning will be explained through a sixfold analysis.
First, the explanation of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Second, the establishment;
third, the enumeration of the three phrases;
fourth, the opening and closing [of categories].
Fifth, the integration;
sixth, the classification according to the teachings.
Within the first section, there are two parts.
First, the names are listed;
second, their characteristics are explained.
Regarding the initial listing of the names:
That is to say, all causes possess six characteristics:
first, being empty yet possessing power without depending on conditions;
second, being empty yet possessing power while depending on conditions.
Third, the three emptinesses are powerless and depend on conditions;
fourth, existence is powerful and does not depend on conditions;
fifth, existence is powerful and depends on conditions.
Sixth, there is the lack of power to wait for conditions.
Regarding the second, the explanation of the characteristics:
the first refers to the meaning of momentary extinction (*kṣaṇabhanga*).
Why is this? Because of momentary cessation,
it is revealed that there is no intrinsic nature.
This is emptiness.
Because it ceases by means of this, the resultant phenomena are able to arise;
this is its efficacy.
However, since this cessation does not occur through the power of conditions,
it is said to be "independent of conditions.
Second, it has the sense of being "coexistent" (sahabhū).
Why is this? Because it exists only through co-existence;
this reveals the meaning that it is non-existent and empty.
Because they coexist, they are capable of accomplishing existence; this is their possession of power.
Because they coexist, they are not isolated; this is their dependence on conditions.
Third, this refers to the meaning of depending upon various conditions.
Why is this? Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty;
because it arises through conditions rather than arising from causes, it is devoid of power.
It is precisely for this reason that it depends upon conditions.
Fourth is the meaning of determination. Why is this so?
It has the sense of "being" because it does not change from its own kind;
it has the sense of "power" because it can produce an effect while remaining unchanged in itself.
However, this non-alteration does not arise through the power of conditions;
thus, it means not depending on conditions.
Fifth is the meaning of drawing forth its own result.
Why is this? Because it has the sense of being "powerful" insofar as it draws forth and manifests its own result.
Although it arises only by depending on conditions,
it does not produce a fruit from those conditions;
this is the meaning of its possessing power.
It is precisely for this reason that it has the meaning of "depending on conditions.
The number six has the meaning of "constantly following along. Why is this so?
Because it follows after others, it cannot be non-existent;
because it cannot contravene conditions, it lacks independent causal efficacy.
It is for this very reason that it is dependent upon conditions.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* speaks in verse to reveal these six meanings:
"Momentary destruction, coexistence, constant following, dependence on various conditions, determination, and the capacity to draw forth only its own fruit; this should be known."
Regarding the second establishment:
one asks why it is definitively stated that there are six meanings and not increased to seven.
"Is it not reduced to five?
Answer: "In order to correspond with the primary cause (hetu) and its conditions (pratyaya), there are only three meanings."
A single cause possesses power independently of conditions because it produces the entire effect; thus,
it is not mixed with the power of conditions.
Second, the causes possess power and depend upon conditions,
as they mutually assist one another to bring about the result.
Third, the causes lack power and depend upon conditions.
Because nothing at all is produced;
because it returns to conditions;
and furthermore, because each of the three aforementioned meanings within the cause possesses two further meanings.
That is to say, there are the meaning of emptiness and the meaning of existence;
each of these two gates has three meanings.
Since there are only six [meanings], they neither increase nor decrease.
Question: Why is the fourth alternative—that which is powerless and does not depend on conditions—not established?
Answer: It is not established because it does not possess the meaning of a cause;
this can be seen upon reflection.
Question: What kind of conditions does "depending on conditions" refer to?
Answer: It refers to the three conditions—namely, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and so forth—external to the causal entity itself.
It does not mean that the six meanings [of the dependent nature] depend upon one another.
Question: It is said that there are six meanings when considering conditions (*pratyaya*) in relation to causes (*hetu*).
I do not yet know whether conditions, when contrasted with causes, also possess these six meanings.
Answer: In this regard, there are two meanings.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) possesses six characteristics in relation to its own dominant fruit,
because it is subsumed under the category of direct causes. However,
in relation to other fruits, it constitutes a remote condition and therefore does not possess all six characteristics.
The same applies to the immediate cause (samanantara-pratyaya) when it anticipates another.
Question: Are there six meanings within the fruit?
Answer: Within the fruit, there are only two meanings: emptiness and existence.
This means that because it arises from others and lacks intrinsic nature,
it has the meaning of emptiness;
yet because it exists as a response to causes, it has the meaning of existence.
If explained according to the principle of mutual causality,
when this single dharma serves as a cause for another, it possesses these six characteristics;
when it acts as a fruit for another, it possesses only two characteristics.
Therefore, these six meanings exist only within the cause.
Question: If that is so, does the present activity serve as the causal seed?
How could there be the six meanings?
Answer: Because the superior conditions are not fully present, as stated in the treatise.
The seed-syllable (bīja) has six meanings;
this is according to the initial teaching (ādikarmika).
As for the secret meaning of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda):
All of these possess these six meanings.
According to the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya),
within this teaching, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses and so forth [are included].
This is also the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha following conditions;
it has no separate self-nature.
Therefore, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses also possess the six meanings found within the fundamental consciousness.
This can be seen by reflecting upon it.
Regarding the third phrase, there are two types of numerical analysis (*vicaya*):
first, that which pertains to the essence (*tattva*).
Second, regarding function; first, regarding the existence or non-existence of the essence, there are four propositions.
The first is "existence," which refers to the sense of certainty.
The second is non-existence,
which refers to the meaning of momentary cessation.
The third is both existence and non-existence.
This refers to the non-duality of that which draws forth its own fruit and that which is co-existent.
Fourth is neither existence nor non-existence;
this refers to the non-duality of that which constantly evolves in accordance [with conditions] and that which depends upon various conditions.
Regarding the use of the four lines:
because that which is constantly evolving and that which depends on various conditions are non-dual when combined,
it does not arise from itself.
Because it is conjoined with that momentary destruction and the certainty of non-duality,
there is no production from another.
Because it is conjoined with that coexistence and the drawing forth of its own fruit in non-duality, [there is no production from another].
It does not arise without causes,
for it is only when the three conditions are present and the six meanings are combined that the sense of "cause" is established;
thus, it is not produced without a cause.
Thus, by means of these six meanings,
the causal conditions are completely set aside to reveal the supreme excellence of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
Therefore, the *Dilun* states:
Causes do not arise because they arise dependently; conditions do not arise because they arise dependently.
Because it arises from its own causes,
it does not arise through co-origination;
because there is no cognizer.
Because it does not abide at the time of its formation,
it is not without cause;
because its arising conforms to existence, it is not non-existent.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Because they exist within their own seeds, they do not arise from another;
because they depend upon various conditions, they do not arise from themselves."
Because they lack causal agency (*kāritra*), they do not arise together;
because they possess functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), they do not arise without a cause.
Question: How do these six meanings relate to the eightfold demarcation (*apratiniyama*)?
Answer: The "Eight Negations" (aṣṭāvakṣara) do not rely on negation but are concerned with manifestation;

furthermore, the "Eight Negations" manifest the principle through its opposite, whereas the "Six Principles" rely on the manifestation of the principle so that conceptual attachment naturally vanishes.
There are these two attendants.
Regarding the fourth point, "opening and closing," it may be understood as being unique in its essence.
Because the cause has no dual nature,
or because it is divided into two according to its meaning—
that is, emptiness and existence.
Because they lack intrinsic nature and because dependent origination is manifest,

The reason these two gates exist is that all phenomena of dependent origination possess two meanings:
first, the meaning of emptiness and existence.
This refers to the meaning of having power or lacking power in relation to its own essence;

By virtue of the first meaning, they attain mutual identity;

This is because, in the former and the latter cases, when the self exists, the other must necessarily be absent.
Therefore, the other is indeed the self.
Why? Because that which is other lacks intrinsic nature, as it is produced by the self.
Second, because when the self is empty, the other must necessarily exist as the self; thus, the self is the other.
Why? Because the self lacks intrinsic nature and is produced by means of the other.
Because the two kinds of existence and the two kinds of emptiness do not coexist with one another,

That which is called "one" is not one by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),

Therefore, that there are ten within one means that they are established through conditions;

Intrinsic nature has no conditions of dependent origination and thus cannot be designated as "one.

Among these ten, there is one which is the "lack of intrinsic nature through dependent origination" (*paratantra-niḥsvabhāvatā*);

what is the use of the other gates?
Answer: The other gates are like space.
Why? Because a single gate of the same essence encompasses everything without exception.
Question: Regarding that which is subsumed within this "identity" (sameness of essence), it should only subsume everything within its own category;
how could it possibly subsume everything within other categories?
The answer is: Since it already encompasses all things within itself, it further encompasses the inexhaustible entirety within each and every other gate;
thus, in successive layers, it exhausts the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Why is this? Because in the perfectly interfused dharma-realm of inexhaustible dependent origination,
there is not a single thing that does not simultaneously become all things.
This is because it discusses only the actual virtues of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
thus, its limits and measure cannot be described.
Therefore, a verse in this sutra says:
Throughout unspeakable eons, one may expound all that is unspeakable;
yet even those unspeakable eons might come to an end.
That which is ineffable cannot be fully expressed.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"The minds of all sentient beings..."
All can be distinguished and known;
even the atoms within all lands may still have their number calculated.
The realm of empty space in the ten directions may still be measured by a single hair;
yet the ultimate realization of a bodhisattva’s initial resolve can never be fathomed.
This is precisely because, through this Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle—which is perfectly consummate, sovereign, and unimpeded—one attains all by attaining one;
thus, cause and effect are simultaneous, without distinction of before or after.
Therefore, the *Dilun* states:
"From the bodhisattvas on the stage of faith up to the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, they constitute a single dependent origination,
which is encompassed by means of the six characteristics, such as the general and the particular."
One clearly knows that cause and effect are simultaneous, mutually compatible, and mutually identical;
each encompasses all others, acting as both principal and attendant to one another.
One must contemplate this deeply; there is no doubt about it.
Furthermore, this sutra says:
"Why is this? Because a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind for enlightenment is himself a Buddha."
They are entirely equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
they are also equal to the spheres of activity of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
and they are entirely equal to the True Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
One attains the Tathāgata’s single body that is immeasurable bodies, and the equal wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
All sentient beings to be transformed are likewise entirely equal.
It is further said:
At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening;
endowed with the body of wisdom, one realizes it through no other means.
Such instances are immeasurable, and so forth.
This is as detailed in the sūtra text.
Question: These [verses] merely praise the virtues within the causal stage;
how can they possibly constitute the fruition of perfected virtue?
Answer: This explains the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Cause and effect are of the same substance, forming a single dependent origination;
to attain this is to attain that.
Because these two are mutually identical,
if the fruit is not obtained, the cause cannot be established as a cause. Why is this so?
It is not that the non-attainment of the fruit and so forth are not causes.
Question: Above it was stated that the characteristics of the fruit's separation from conditions cannot be explained;
why then is only the division of the cause discussed?
Why is it that at the final stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one immediately explains the dharma of attaining the fruit of becoming a Buddha?
Answer: To say that one "becomes a Buddha" means...
From the very first moment of seeing and hearing [the Dharma],
up until the second birth, one attains the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*).
When the final moment of mind in this stage of practice reaches its ultimate fulfillment, the causal state is perfected.
In the third birth, one immediately attains that ultimate, sovereign, and perfectly integrated fruit.
Because the substance of this cause is established in dependence upon the fruit,
those whose cause is fulfilled simply vanish into the ocean of the fruit.
Because this is a realm realized through direct testimony,
it cannot be described.
This is as in the cases of the Dragon Girl, the youth Viśvavyūha, Sudhana, and the devaputra from Tuṣita Heaven, and others.
Regarding the meaning that one attains that fruit within three lifetimes, and so forth, it should be understood in detail according to the explanations in the sūtras.
Question: As stated above, one can attain Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.
Question: This meaning already exists within the Three Vehicles;
how does this differ from them?
Answer: It is because the Three Vehicles are viewed from the perspective of principle (li).
By means of a single thought-moment, one immediately attains Buddhahood.
Now, this One Vehicle (Ekayāna) fully possesses all teachings and meanings within a single thought-moment.
All dharmas such as principle and phenomena, cause and effect, and so forth,

as well as all sentient beings, shall simultaneously, simultaneously, simultaneously, simultaneously, simultaneously, simultaneously, simultaneously, simultaneously, simultaneously, simultaneously attain Buddhahood.
Thereafter, they all newly and continuously sever their delusions;
furthermore, they do not abide in the stage of training (śaikṣa-bhūmi) when attaining perfect enlightenment.
This is because they are fully endowed with the ten buddha-qualities to manifest inexhaustible virtues of both adverse and favorable conditions.
Furthermore, the subtle Indra [samādhi] pervades all stages throughout nine and ten lifetimes;
that is to say, it is taught to extend from the final moment of the ten levels of faith (daśa-śraddhā) onwards through the ten understandings (daśa-adhimukti),
the ten practices (daśa-caryā), the ten dedications (daśa-pariṇāmanā), the ten stages (daśa-bhūmi), and up to the Buddha stage (buddha-bhūmi).
Simultaneously and universally accomplished without before or after,
it is fully endowed with all things. Yet,
this single thought-moment is no different from hundreds of thousands of eons.
You must reflect upon this directly.
This concludes the third gate, the Gate of the Mutual Identity and Sovereignty of All Dharmas.
The fourth is the Gate of the Realm of Indra’s Net.
This merely differs from the preceding through its metaphorical illustration.
The essential substance and characteristics of all these meanings above are sovereign;
their concealment and manifestation appear to one another in infinite, overlapping layers.
Therefore, this sutra says:
"Within a single atom,
each displays nayutas of countless billions of Buddhas preaching the Dharma therein."
Within a single mote of dust,
he manifests immeasurable Buddha-lands with Mount Sumerus and adamantine encircling walls;
yet the world is not cramped.
Within a single atom,
there appear the three evil realms, as well as devas and asuras, each receiving their respective retributions.
These three verses refer to the three worlds.
It is further said:
"Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields sit within a single pore."
In each there are immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattvas,
who each fully expound the practices of Samantabhadra;
immeasurable oceans of lands reside within a single hair-pore.
They sit entirely upon the lotus thrones of enlightenment, pervading all realms of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
manifesting with sovereign mastery from every pore.
It is further said:
Just as it is manifested in a single atom, so it is in all atoms;
the rest is as described extensively in the sutra, being immeasurable and beyond reckoning.
These are all actual realities and not transformations.
This refers to the objects of the *yathābhūta-pramāṇa* (cognition of things as they are) within the *yathābhūta-jñāna* (wisdom of suchness).
Other transformations and the like do not fall under this category.
Why is this? Because these are all the true virtues of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
it is simply the natural order of things.
This does not refer to the objects of discriminating emotional consciousness;
these can be eliminated by reflecting upon them.
Question: Regarding the statement that within a single mote of dust there appear immeasurable Buddha-fields, and so forth—
This is merely a single layer of manifestation.
Why, then, is it said that there are "repeated layers" of manifestation?
The answer is: this is precisely when the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is being expounded.
It is said that within all atoms it is likewise taught; when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is taught within those atoms, it is also said that within all atoms it is likewise taught.
In this manner, they unfold successively, becoming ever more profound and inexhaustible.
One should reflect upon this accordingly.
Question: If, according to this text, they are thus successively unfolding and inexhaustible, [how is this so?]
What is their limit, and how are their beginning and end distinguished?
Answer: They are grasped according to one's wisdom;
taking one as the primary focus, the others serve as its companions.
That which occupies the head position is the central deity;
the others are the retinue surrounding them,
as described in the aforementioned teachings and principles.
All are thus spontaneously accomplished through mastery.
Reversing the preceding characteristics, they enter one another with sovereign ease;
in this manner, all phenomena are subsumed within the inexhaustible dharma-realm, all of which are established as Indra-like.
Fifth is the gate of subtle mutual containment and establishment.

Within a single moment of thought, all these aforementioned meanings are fully present— encompassing all dharma-gates such as beginning and end, simultaneity and succession, anteriority and posteriority, and direct and reverse order.
Within a single thought-moment, they manifest simultaneously and all at once with such clarity that nothing remains obscure;
it is just as if a bundle of arrows were displayed all at once.
Therefore, this sutra says:
In a single thought-moment,
the Bodhisattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb,
and so forth, until the dissemination of the śarīra and the long endurance of the Dharma.
Furthermore, all the sentient beings who are benefited thereby are manifested within a single thought-moment,
as described in detail in the sutra text.
It is further said:
Within a single pore, immeasurable Buddha-fields—
adorned, pure, and vast— abide in perfect tranquility.
It is further said:
"Within a single atom,
there are subtle lands."
All atoms and so forth abide entirely within it;
this should be contemplated according to reason.
Question: How does this meaning differ from the aforementioned Indra?
Answer: They are layered and interwoven, appearing in mutual reflection.
The Indra-net (Indra-jāla) is brilliantly manifest as a whole, while the subtle net is contained within it.
These various meanings are all distinct and different from one another.
One should reflect upon this carefully.
Sixth is the gate of the simultaneous accomplishment of the secret and the manifest.
All the meanings mentioned above are both concealed and revealed.
They are accomplished simultaneously.
Therefore, this sutra says:
"In this very place, one enters right concentration."
From another direction, one arises from samādhi;
the eye-faculty enters right concentration;
the object of form arises from samādhi, and so forth.
It is further stated:
"One enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) within a male body and arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within a female body," and so forth.
Entering meditative absorption within a single atom,
they emerge from samādhi on the tip of a single hair;
thus, while this remains hidden, that becomes manifest.
The secret perfection of entering meditative absorption and emerging from it simultaneously is thus established.
Furthermore, this sutra states:
"Because there are those with whom one has a karmic affinity throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
Coming and going, entering and exiting, they deliver sentient beings;
some see the Bodhisattva entering meditative absorption,
while others see the Bodhisattva arising from concentration.
It is further said: Within those worlds of the ten directions,

in every moment of thought, he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of the True Dharma, the entry into nirvana, and the distribution of relics, thereby delivering sentient beings.
Thus it is immeasurable,
as explained at length in the sutras.
Furthermore, it is as when the Buddha conferred predictions upon the various bodhisattvas.
There are those who receive the prediction of enlightenment in their presence, and those who receive it secretly without being present;
as explained above in the first coin, these ten coins are termed "manifest."
Regarding the second coin in relation to the first coin, the ten [aspects] therein constitute the secret.
Why is this? Because one perceives this but does not perceive that.
Because they do not cognize one another;
although they do not cognize or see one another,
nevertheless, this is established because that is established.
Both are termed "accomplishment.
One should reflect upon this accordingly.
Seventh is the gateway of the various treasuries possessing both pure and mixed virtues.
The various meanings above are either pure or mixed,
as in the case of the preceding discussion on persons and dharmas.
If one approaches them from the perspective of the person (pudgala):
Because all are exclusively human beings, it is called "pure" (śuddha).
Furthermore, because this very category of humans encompasses all differentiated phenomena, such as principle and phenomena, it is called "mixed" (miśra).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva enters a single samādhi and practices only giving—immeasurable and boundless, with no other practices—it is called "pure.
Moreover, upon entering a single samādhi, they simultaneously practice the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, and the saving of sentient beings.
Countless and boundless other miscellaneous practices are all accomplished simultaneously.
Thus, the phenomena of the dharma-realm arise in profusion, with mastery over both purity and impurity.
There is nothing that is not fully complete;
you should reflect upon this accordingly.
Eighth is the gate of the distinct accomplishment of the ten worlds separated by time.
All these various meanings above manifest simultaneously and distinctly throughout the ten periods of time,
because time and phenomena are inseparable.
Regarding the "ten periods":
each of the three periods— past, future,
and present— has its own past, future, and present.
This constitutes nine periods of time.
However, because these nine periods mutually interpenetrate one another,
they form a single comprehensive statement.
The general and the particular together constitute the ten times.
These ten times are fully endowed with distinct differences;
because they manifest simultaneously, they form dependent origination.
To "attain" means to enter immediately.
Therefore, this sutra says:
"Or by means of long kalpas, one enters short kalpas."
A short eon enters into a long eon;
alternatively, hundreds of thousands of great eons become a single thought-moment,
and a single thought-moment is itself hundreds of thousands of great eons.
Or they enter past kalpas into future kalpas,
and future kalpas into past kalpas;
thus they possess mastery over time and kalpas without obstruction.
The mutual identity and mutual interpenetration of phenomena are thus perfectly integrated.
Furthermore, this sutra states:
"Within a single atom..."
He universally manifests all Buddha-fields of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, it is said:
within a single atom.
He universally manifests before all sentient beings of the three periods of time.
It is further said:
"Within a single mote of dust..."
Universally manifesting all the buddha-activities of the three periods of time.
It is further said:
"Within a single mote of dust."
They establish the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
such instances are immeasurable,
as detailed extensively in the sutra text.
This universally encompasses all the aforementioned thematic gateways,
manifesting with sovereign mastery throughout the ten periods of time;
one should reflect upon this accordingly.
Ninth is the gate of the excellent accomplishment through the turning of mind-only.
All the meanings mentioned above are nothing other than this single *tathāgatagarbha*.
It is the transformation of the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*). However,
because its nature arises endowed with all virtues,
it differs from the Three Vehicles.
However, a single mind is also fully endowed with ten kinds of virtues;
this refers precisely to what is taught in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" regarding the meaning of the ten minds and so forth.
The reason ten are mentioned is to manifest their inexhaustibility.
Thus, these sovereign powers are fully endowed with an infinite variety of virtues.
All these aforementioned categories of meaning are entirely the sovereign functions of this mind;
there is nothing else that can be called "the transformation of mind-only" or the like.
One should consider how to explain this.
Tenth is the gate of generating understanding by entrusting phenomena to manifest the Dharma.
All the meanings above follow the phenomena to which they are entrusted.
This refers to the distinct manifestation of specific phenomena,
namely all dharma-gates such as principles and matters. For instance,
the descriptions of the characteristics of ten kinds of jewel-king clouds and so forth mentioned in this sutra.
This refers to the various dharma-gates.
Because the aforementioned meanings are noble and precious,
the term "jewel" (ratna) is established to represent them.
The term "King" is designated to signify that it exercises sovereign mastery over the aforementioned meanings;
it is designated to signify that it provides nourishment and benefit to the aforementioned meanings.
Because he provided sustenance and grace,
and because he was ever-vigilant,
he was designated by the symbol of the cloud.
Such matters as these are immeasurable, as should be reflected upon according to the sūtras.
Question: This principle exists within the Three Vehicles.
How does this differ from that?
Answer: The three vehicles rely on distinct phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) to manifest distinct principles;
now, in this single vehicle (*ekayāna*), the phenomenal characteristics upon which it relies—
This is precisely the principle manifested therein;
there is nothing else.
It fully encompasses all principles and phenomena, teachings and meanings, as well as the aforementioned dharma-gates.
There is nothing that is not fully encompassed herein.
It is fitting that one should reflect upon this according to the principle.
The above constitutes the explanation of these ten gates.
Together with the ten meanings and so forth from the preceding main text,
they are all simultaneously integrated and harmonized to form the gateway of the single dharma-realm dependent origination endowed with all virtues.
When observing the realm of the Universal Eye with discernment at other times,
one abides solely within a mind of great understanding, great practice,
and great vision and hearing. Yet, within each of these ten gates, all the others are subsumed without exception.
One should harmonize and integrate [these points] through the skillful means of the six characteristics; this may be inferred accordingly.
All that has been explained above is merely a brief manifestation of the meaning of dependent origination within the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, within this context, other characteristics of phenomena, as well as questions and answers for dispelling doubts,
may be either identical to or different from those of the three vehicles;
these are designated and established as skillful means (*upāya*) and the like.
These have been explained extensively in the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the sutras and śāstras, as well as in the *Kongmu* and the *Wenda*.
They are entirely distinct and different from those of the Three Vehicles;
one should accordingly contemplate them by relying extensively upon the "Universal Eye Realm" (*Puyan jingjie*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Question: The principle set forth above differs from that of the Three Vehicles; this may indeed be accepted as credible.
However, by what textual authority is it proven that there exists a distinct One Vehicle (Ekayāna) outside of the Three Vehicles?
Answer: This sutra itself contains explicit text;
thus, a verse says:
"All classes of sentient beings in all worlds..."
Those who seek the path of the śrāvaka are few;
those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha are even fewer still;
and those who seek the Mahāyāna are exceedingly rare.
To seek the Mahāyāna is still relatively easy;
however, to be able to believe in this Dharma is exceedingly difficult.
This is because this Dharma transcends the mundane mind and is thus hard to believe.
Therefore, the Noble One compared those three vehicles to one another to resolve this.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"If there are sentient beings who are inferior and whose minds are weary and despondent..."
To demonstrate the path of the śrāvaka and cause one to emerge from all sufferings is the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings whose faculties are only slightly clear and sharp,
yet who delight in the Dharma of causes and conditions.
For them, he teaches the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
which is the middle vehicle.
This is for those whose faculties are clear and sharp.
Possessing a heart of great compassion,
he benefits all sentient beings by expounding the path of the bodhisattva.
This is precisely the Mahāyāna.
If one possesses the unsurpassed mind and is resolutely intent upon the great task, [one should practice this].
To manifest the Buddha-body and to preach the inexhaustible Buddha-dharma is the One Vehicle.
Because this Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) cannot be received by those of inferior capacity,
the Great Sage, through his skillful means,
provisionally taught it in small measure according to their respective capacities and inclinations within the context of the Three Vehicles.
Because they have not yet fathomed the source of the Dharma-realm,
[the Buddhas] provisionally manifest as two bodies, three bodies,
and so forth. Now, for those with such supreme mental capacity who delight in the Great Matter, the Buddha has finally manifested the realm of the ten bodies.
This refers to preaching the inexhaustible Buddha-dharma;
it is called manifesting the Buddha-body to preach the inexhaustible Buddha-dharma.
The three vehicles merely accord with the capacities of beings.
Because it does not yet manifest the self-realized realm of the ten bodies of all Buddhas,
it is not the manifestation of the Buddha-body.
Furthermore, it teaches according to the capacities of beings, briefly explaining a single characteristic, a single tranquility, and the principle of a single flavor.
This is not an exhaustive explanation.
Why? Because for the three vehicles, this infinity is considered a fault;
however, for this single vehicle, it is regarded as a true virtue.
Furthermore, this sutra states:
"In a single world-system,
those who hear the teaching of the One Vehicle."
There may be two, three, four, five, or even an infinite number of vehicles;
this is merely stated according to the distinctions between the fundamental and the derivative.
The words and meanings of the holy teachings are clearly evident.
One must not be startled or find it strange by clinging to one's own subjective sentiments.
Fourth, the meaning of the perfect interfusion of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).
This is analyzed through three gates regarding the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the six characteristics.
First, the enumeration of names and brief explanation;
second, clarifying the intent for the emergence of the teaching;
third, the detailed explanation through questions and answers.
Regarding the initial listing of names:

these are the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the common characteristic (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*), the distinct characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of formation (*saṃbhava-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of disintegration (*vibhava-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the general characteristic:
Because it is a single *śata* (hundred) of qualities;
as for its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
the many qualities are not one.
Because the particular bases, by means of inference, fulfill that totality. As for "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):
it refers to many meanings that do not contradict one another.
Because they collectively constitute a single totality.
As for their distinct characteristics,
it is because when multiple meanings are compared with one another, each is mutually different.
The characteristic of formation refers to the fact that these various conditions arise and come into being.
The characteristic of disintegration refers to...
Because all phenomena abide in their own respective natures without shifting,
the purpose of the second teaching is to reveal the infinite,

perfectly interfused, and sovereign characteristics of the *dharmadhātu* dependent origination of the One Vehicle; it reveals their mutual identity, non-obstruction, seamless integration, and even the inexhaustible principle and phenomena of the *indrala* [net] array.
When this meaning manifests, all afflictive obstructions are severed once and for all;
one attains the cessation of the afflictions of nine or ten lifetimes.
In the practice of virtue, the one is accomplished and all are accomplished;
in the principle of nature, the one is manifested and all are manifested.
Both the universal and the particular are fully endowed, being equal from beginning to end.
At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening.
This is truly because the six characteristics of the dependent origination of the dharma-realm are thus fused together;
cause and effect are simultaneous, their mutual identity is sovereign, and they fully encompass both the reverse and the direct orders.
The cause is the universal practice and realization of Samantabhadra,
while the result is the infinite manifestation of the realm of the ten Buddhas,
as extensively explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Regarding the third section, the explanation through questions and answers:
although the principle of dependent origination applies universally across all contexts,
for now we shall briefly explain it by means of the example of a house constructed through conditions.
Question: What is the general characteristic?
Answer: It is the house.
Question: Is this merely the rafters and other such conditions?
What is the house?
The answer is: the rafters are the house. Why is this so?
Because the rafters alone are fully capable of forming a house;
if separated from the rafters, the house is not established,
yet when the rafters are obtained, the house is obtained.
Question: If the rafters were entirely capable of constructing the house by themselves, then even in the absence of tiles and other materials, they should still be able to construct it.
Answer: When tiles and other materials are absent, they are not yet "rafters," and therefore they do not construct it.
It is not that the rafter is incapable of acting;
rather, when we say it "can act," we are simply discussing the rafter's capacity to act.
It is not said that it is not made by the rafters. Why?
Because the rafters are the causal conditions.
Because there is no causal condition at the time when the relinquishing has not yet been accomplished, it is not a condition.
If it were the rafter, it would already be fully completed.
If it is not fully completed, it cannot be called a rafter.
Question: If various conditions such as rafters each exert a small amount of power and together perform an incomplete action, [how can there be a result]?
What fault is there? The answer is: there would be the faults of nihilism and eternalism.
If [the cause] were not fully established but possessed only slight power, [these faults would follow].
The various conditions each possess but little power;
since this [result] is merely many instances of little power and does not constitute a single,
complete whole, it is therefore "annihilated."
Since all conditions are weak and none possess complete efficacy,
those who maintain that something exists as a whole while being abandoned [by its parts] are asserting that it is eternal, because it exists without cause.
If it were not fully completed,
then even when one rafter was removed, the house should still remain;
yet, since the house is not fully completed, [it does not exist].
Therefore, we know that it is not the case that a small amount of effort can bring about complete perfection.
Question: When there is not even a single roof-tile, is that not a house?
Answer: It is merely a ruined house; there is no good house.
Thus we know that the preference for the house belongs entirely to a single rafter.
Since it belongs to a single rafter,
we know that the rafter is itself the house.
Question: If the roof-ridge is identical to the rafters, then should the other wooden boards, tiles, and so forth also be identical to the rafters?
Answer: In their totality, they are all indeed rafters.
Why is this? Because if the rafters are removed, there is no house.
The reason for this is as follows:
If there are no rafters, the house will collapse.
Because the house collapses, the boards, tiles, and so forth cannot be called such;
therefore, the boards, tiles, and so forth are themselves the rafters.
If the rafters do not immediately exist,
the house will not be completed;
the rafters, tiles, and all other components likewise will not be completed.
Now that both have been established,
we know they are mutually identical.
If this is so for a single rafter, it holds for all.
The same applies to all other rafters.
Therefore, regarding all dependently originated phenomena (pratītyasamutpāda-dharma), it is either that they do not arise at all, or if they do arise,
their characteristics are mutually identical.
Melted and fused, unimpeded, sovereign, and perfectly consummate;
inconceivable and transcending the limits of conceptual cognition,
this principle of the dependent origination of dharmatā is to be understood accordingly in all instances.
Second, regarding specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*):
because the various conditions, such as the rafters and so forth,
are distinct from the whole, if they were not distinct, the meaning of the "whole" would not be established.
Because there is no whole without its parts,
what does this mean? It is precisely by means of the parts that the whole is established.
Because there is no distinction, the general cannot be established.
Therefore, that which is particular is precisely what establishes the particular by means of the general.
Question: If the general is identical to the particular, would it not follow that the general cannot be established?
Answer: It is because the general is identical to the particular.
Therefore, the general [characteristic] is established.
For example, because a rafter is itself a house, it is called the general characteristic;
because it is itself a rafter, it is called the specific characteristic.
If it were not immediately the rafters, it would not be the house;
if it were not immediately the rafters, it would not be the house.
One should reflect upon this identity of the general and the particular.
Question: If the characteristics are identical, why are they said to be distinct?
Answer: It is precisely because the characteristics are identical that they constitute distinctness.
If they were not mutually identical,
then because the whole would exist outside of the parts, it would not be the whole;
and because the parts would exist outside of the whole, they would not be parts.
This can be understood through reflection.
Question: If they are not distinct, what fault ensues?
Answer: There would be the fault of [falling into] nihilism or eternalism.
If there were no distinction [between them],
then there would be no distinct rafters and tiles;
because there would be no distinct rafters and tiles.
In that case, it would not constitute the abandonment of the house as a whole;
for if there were a house as a whole even in the absence of individual rafters, tiles, and so forth, [it would be untenable].
To have a house without causes would be the error of permanence.
Regarding the third point, the common characteristic:
the rafters and other various conditions combine in harmony to produce the house.
Because they are not mutually contradictory, they are all termed "conditions for equanimity" (upekṣā-ālambana).
It is not because they produce other things that they are called "common characteristics" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).
Question: What is the difference between these and "general characteristics" (saṃgraha-lakṣaṇa)?
Answer: The general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is explained solely with reference to the single house.
Here, this common characteristic (*samānalakṣaṇa*) refers to the various conditions such as the rafters;
although their substances are each distinct, they are called "common characteristics" because the meaning of their functional efficacy is equal.
Question: If they are not identical, what fault would there be?
Answer: If they were not identical, there would be the faults of nihilism and eternalism. Why is this so?
If they were not identical,
then the rafters and other components would be mutually contradictory and unable to function together as a house;
since the house could not exist, this would constitute annihilationism.
If one does not perform the act of relinquishing that which is contrary [to it],
yet clings to the existence of relinquishment,
then because there would be relinquishment without a cause, it would be permanent.

The fourth [point], regarding distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*), is that the various conditions, such as rafters and so forth, are mutually differentiated according to their respective forms and types.
Question: If they are distinct, should they not be different?
Answer: It is precisely because they are different that they are identical.
If they were not different, since the rafter is already one zhang two chi long, [the other members would likewise be so].
The same should apply to the tiles;
because they destroy the fundamental conditions of the dharma,
they lose the prior meaning of constituting a house through their uniformity.
Now that it has been established that they are abandoned, one should know that those which share the same name, "condition," are actually distinct.
Question: What is the difference between these and the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)?
Answer: Regarding the aforementioned specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
it is because the rafters and other various conditions are distinct from the single house that they are called "specific characteristics."
Now, as for "distinct characteristics":
the various conditions, such as the rafters and so forth,
each possess distinct characteristics when viewed in relation to one another.
Question: If they are not different, what fault is there?
Answer: There is the fault of [falling into] the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.
Why is this? If they were not different,
then the tile would be identical to the rafter, which is twelve feet long.
If one destroys the dharma of fundamental conditions and thus fails to achieve the house, it is annihilationism.
If one fails to achieve the house through conditions yet clings to the existence of a house,
then because the house exists without a cause, it is eternalism.
The fifth is the characteristic of establishment.
Because the meaning of relinquishing is established by means of these various conditions,
and because relinquishing is thus established.
The rafters and so forth are called conditions (*pratyaya*).
If it were not so, neither of the two would be established.
Since they are now seen to be established, we know that characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) mutually establish one another.
Question: We directly perceive various conditions such as rafters and so forth, each abiding in its own nature and originally not constituting a house.
For what reason can the meaning of a "house" be established?
Answer: It is precisely because the rafters and other various conditions do not act that the meaning of "house" is established. Why is this so?
If the rafters were to depart from the house,
they would immediately lose their nature as rafters; consequently,
the meaning of "house" could not be established.
Now, because [the action] was not performed,
and because conditions such as the rafters and so forth are present,
it is due to this presence that [the result arises].
The meaning of "abandoning" (prahāṇa) is thus established.
Furthermore, if one does not construct the rafters and so forth, they would not be called "multiple conditions" (bahupratyaya);
since they are now designated as "conditions," [the term "abandoning" is justified].
Knowing for certain that it has been relinquished.
Question: If it is not established, what fault is there?
Answer: There would be the faults of annihilationism and eternalism. Why?
Because it is established by depending on its original causes and conditions, such as the rafters and so forth.
Since neither of these is performed now,
there can be no relinquishing;
therefore, this is cessation.
Originally, rafters are named as such because they constitute a house through conditions;
now, since they no longer form a house, the rafters do not exist, which is annihilation.
If they were not so constituted, the house would exist without a cause, and thus it would be eternal.
Furthermore, that the rafters do not produce the designation "rafter" while yet being designated as rafters would also imply they are eternal.
As for the sixth characteristic of disintegration:
because the various conditions, such as the rafters, each abide in their own intrinsic nature and do not originate [as such], [they are disintegrating].
Question: We clearly see that various conditions, such as rafters and so forth, bring about the completion of a house.
Why, then, do you say that it was not made originally?
Answer: It is precisely because it was not made [by a creator] that it exists.

The act of relinquishing is established [only] when one departs from the dharma. If one performs the relinquishment but does not depart from one's own dharma, the meaning of relinquishing is not established. Why is this?
Because [the act] was performed as a formal abandonment, the relinquishment was not accomplished;
now that the relinquishment is accomplished,
it is clearly known that no further action is required.
Question: If it is said that "the rafters go to make the house," what fault is there?
Answer: There are two faults, namely those of annihilationism and eternalism.
If one says, "the rafters go to make the house," [it follows these faults].
Then the dharma of the rafters is lost.
Because the dharma of the rafters is lost,
the house would then lack rafters and could not exist.
This is annihilation.
If there were a house that existed apart from the principle of the rafters,
then a house existing without rafters would be permanent.
Furthermore, the general is the single house;
the particular is the various conditions;
and their sameness is that they do not contradict one another.
"Differentiation" refers to the distinctness of the various conditions;
"formation" refers to the various conditions accomplishing the fruit;
and "destruction" refers to each abiding in its own nature.
Another verse says:
The "one" that possesses many names is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); The "many" that are not one is the particular characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Many types, being identical within themselves, constitute the general; Each individual essence, though distinct, appears as identical.
The principle of the dependent origination of the one and the many is subtly established; The destruction and abiding of self-dharmas are eternally uncreated.
This is the realm of wisdom alone, not the consciousness of phenomena. By this expedient means, the One Vehicle is realized.
*Huayan Yicheng Jiaoyi Fenqizhang*, Scroll Four.
